document.title: Revised WHO classification and treatment of childhood pneumonia at health facilities
document.note: Curated evidence snippets for reproducible lightweight retrieval evaluation from the bundled WHO childhood pneumonia guideline PDF.

chunks.text: Children with cough or difficult breathing should be assessed for fast breathing, chest indrawing, and general danger signs to classify pneumonia severity.
Fast breathing pneumonia is classified when a child with cough or difficult breathing has age-specific fast breathing but no chest indrawing and no general danger signs.
Chest indrawing pneumonia is present when a child has cough or difficult breathing with lower chest wall indrawing but no general danger signs.
General danger signs include inability to drink or breastfeed, persistent vomiting, convulsions, lethargy or unconsciousness, and stridor in a calm child.
Oral amoxicillin is recommended as first-line antibiotic treatment for children with fast breathing pneumonia or chest indrawing pneumonia who can be managed as outpatients.
Children with fast breathing pneumonia should receive oral amoxicillin treatment for an appropriate short course according to WHO recommendations.
Children with chest indrawing pneumonia may be treated with oral amoxicillin on an outpatient basis when referral is not required and danger signs are absent.
In settings with high HIV prevalence or known HIV infection or exposure, pneumonia management may require special consideration and broader clinical assessment.
Caregivers should be advised to return for follow-up or immediately if the child becomes sicker, develops danger signs, cannot drink, or has worsening breathing.
Children with severe pneumonia or very severe disease, including danger signs, should receive urgent referral and appropriate pre-referral treatment.
